title: Gog Falls and Israel Comes Home
overview: Ezekiel pictures the LORD destroying the invading army of Gog, Israel cleansing the land of the dead, and every scattered Israelite brought home for good.

parts.label: Gog's army falls (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The LORD brings Gog, a ruler from the far north, to Israel's mountains, knocks the bow and arrows from his hands, and leaves his army dead in the open field. Scholars do not know who Gog was, and translations differ on his title in verse 1: 'prince of Rosh' or 'chief prince' of Meshech and Tubal, lands in what is now Turkey.

parts.label: Weapons become firewood (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: So many weapons are left behind that Israel burns them as fuel for seven years and needs no other wood, and former victims take the goods of those who robbed them. Seven often stands for completeness, so the number likely stresses how total the defeat is and how clearly it shows the LORD's holiness (v. 7).

parts.label: Burying the dead (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Israel's law treated dead bodies as making the land unclean, meaning unfit for worship, so the whole nation spends seven months burying the enemy dead, and then searchers mark even single bones. The mass grave is named Hamon Gog, 'Gog's horde', but where it lies and what 'block the way of travelers' means are unclear, and translations differ there.

parts.label: A feast for scavengers (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: In a grim reversal of a sacrifice, where worshippers ate the offered meat, the LORD invites birds and wild animals to feed on fallen soldiers, pictured as fattened livestock from Bashan, a region famous for cattle. The book of Revelation reuses this scene (Revelation 19), and Christians read it there as part of Jesus's final victory over evil.

parts.label: Why the exile happened (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: As in verse 7, the aim is that the nations see the LORD's power and Israel knows him as its God. The nations will also learn that Israel's exile came from Israel's own unfaithfulness, not from their God's weakness, since 'hid my face' means he withdrew his protection.

parts.label: Brought home for good (vv. 25-29)
parts.note: The LORD promises compassion, a return home with no one left behind, and an end to hiding his face, because he will pour out his Spirit, his own life and presence, on Israel. Translations differ in verse 26, where Israel either 'forgets' or 'bears' its shame, and in verse 29, where the Spirit is either promised or already given.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Gog's invasion is a literal future war, as many who map prophecy onto the end times expect, or a symbolic picture of God finally defeating every power that opposes him, and some older readers linked it to wars already past.
think: This chapter imagines people turning an enemy's weapons into firewood and spending months burying even the enemy dead. What do you think it takes for a community to truly recover after violence?
